# PREVENTION OF VIRAL INFECTIONS IN A PATIENT WITH MALIGNANCY

Viral infections reactivate in a small percentage of people with malignancy.

Most viral infections in patients with hematologic malignancies or solid tumors result from reactivation of asymptomatic latent infections, predominantly of herpes viruses, including herpes simplex virus (HSV), varicella zoster virus (VZV) and cytomegalovirus (CMV). Exogenous respiratory tract infections caused by influenza, parainfluenza or respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) are less common.

The main risk factor for clinically relevant reactivation is profound disruption of cellular immune response, usually due to chemotherapy.

The duration and severity of neutropenia are of lesser importance.

The risk of viral disease increases with the intensity and duration of functional T-cell suppression. Patients receiving conventionally dosed chemotherapy regimens for solid tumors experience no major T-cell suppression and do not have a higher incidence of invasive viral infections.
